teaching.causalExplanation: Here's how a typical plan works. You pay the first instalment today, a hundred and twenty dollars. An instalment is one of the equal payments. Then the plan takes the next three every two weeks, from your card or bank account. So it's paid off in six weeks. Watch what you still owe. Four eighty, three sixty, two forty, one twenty, nothing. The instalments add back to exactly the price, and there's no interest. It's still a kind of credit, because you get the item before you've paid for it. So who pays the provider? Mostly the shop. It pays the provider a small cut of every sale, because people buy more when they don't have to pay all at once. That's worth knowing. These plans are built to make spending easy. The plan can still cost you, through fees. Some plans charge an account fee, a fee for each month you owe them money. Our example plan charges six dollars a month. This plan is open across two months, so that's twelve dollars, and the total cost is four hundred and ninety-two. Other plans charge nothing extra if you pay on time. But almost all of them charge a late fee, a fee each time a payment is missed. In our example plan, it's ten dollars. Miss one payment, and the total becomes five hundred and two. So the total cost is the price, plus any account fees, plus any late fees. Fees differ between plans, and they can change, so read the plan before you tap. And "no interest" doesn't mean no extra cost. Fees aren't interest, but you still pay them. Is twelve dollars a lot? Compare it with the price, just like a percentage change. Twelve divided by four eighty is two and a half per cent. With the late fee, the extra is twenty-two dollars, and twenty-two divided by four eighty is about four point six per cent. One missed payment nearly doubled the extra cost. That's why paying on time is the whole game. On a plan with no account fee, paying on time really does cost nothing extra.

scenes.teachingReason: One plan on its own can look easy. The trouble often starts with several. Say you've got three plans running at once: the headphones at a hundred and twenty a fortnight, shoes at forty-five, and a concert ticket at thirty. That's a hundred and ninety-five dollars every two weeks. If you only have a hundred and fifty spare each fortnight, after rent and food, the payments don't fit. Something gets missed, and the late fees start. Since June twenty twenty-five, these providers need a credit licence and have to check that a plan suits you, and missed payments can show on your credit report. But the simplest check is yours. Add up every plan's payment, and compare it with what you've got spare.
